title: Dawn Song - Towards Building Safe and Secure Agentic AI

segments.text: DAWN SONG: Hi, everyone.
I hope everyone has enjoyed the morning session,
and I'm going to kick off the afternoon session.
Thanks, everyone for being here.
Today, I will talk about towards building
safe and secure agentic AI.
Year 2025 was termed the year of agents,
and this year, we continue to see further explosive growth
of agents.
And on one hand, we want to continue
to enjoy the great benefits brought by these frontier AI
capabilities and agentic AI.
On the other hand, we also need to pay attention
to a broad spectrum of different types of AI risks.
And also in particular, I want to stress
that as we deploy AI in the real world,
it's important to consider the presence of attackers
for a number of reasons.
First, history has shown that attackers always follow
the footsteps of new technology development
and sometimes even leads it.
And also this time, the stake is even higher with AI.
As AI controls more and more systems,
attackers will have a higher and higher incentives
to compromise them.
And also as AI becomes more and more capable,
the consequence of misuse by attackers
will also become more and more severe.
And hence, it's really important to consider agentic AI
in the adversarial setting.
And in particular, the overall goal
we are trying to achieve here is to advance safe and secure AI
innovation to ensure its potential benefits are
responsibly realized and widely shared.
In order to achieve this goal, we
need to develop different types of technical and also
socio-technical solutions to build
safe and secure agentic AI.
And in particular, this is a large domain,
and we need to divide the problems
into different categories.
So the first part I will talk about
is on building secure agentic AI to protect our agentic AI
systems from malicious attacks from attackers.
And second, I will talk about how
we can then, on the other side, mitigate misuse.
In particular, as agentic AI capabilities
continue to increase, we need to be able to mitigate misuse
by attackers.
And in particular, I will focus on the impact
of frontier AI in the landscape of cybersecurity.
So first, let's talk about building secure agentic AI.
Agentic AI systems, they can be very powerful and very dynamic.
The systems they use, for example, large language
models for reasoning, planning, and figuring out
actions or actions to take, use different tools and so on,
and then they allow agents to interact with the environment
to perceive from the environment,
and also take actions in the environment.
And when we talk about safety and security of agentic AI
systems, this actually is much more complex when in the past,
we only talked about AI safety and security at the model
level itself.
At the model level, you give it an input,
a prompt, and you get an output, but with the agentic systems,
the agents can take rich actions,
can have a lot of privileges, and the consequences
of attack and misbehaviors can be much more severe.
So to learn more information about AI safety and security
at the model level, I encourage you to watch my ICLR keynote
last year, but given the interest of time,
for the rest of the talk, I will focus on safety and security
issues of agentic AI at the overall agentic AI system level.
When we talk about agentic AI, we
are not talking about just one single type of agents, actually,
there is a broad design space.
In our recent paper, overviewing the attack and defense landscape
of agentic AI systems, we also outline the overall design space
of agentic AI along multiple dimensions as listed here.
And the point I want to emphasize here
is that along each dimension, as we increase
agent flexibility along each of these dimensions,
including the input trust level, the [? tools ?] workflow,
and so on for the agents, we are also simultaneously increasing
the attack surface.
And overall, again, in our overall paper
overviewing the whole landscape of attack and defense space
for agentic AI, we also identify diverse attack factors
and different types of security risks in the agentic AI space.
And you can check out paper for more details.
And this also is not just theoretical.
In fact, together with the rise of agentic AI,
we are also seeing real world attacks
on agents that's rising fast.
For example, CloutHub for open cloud
already has a significant fraction of its scales
that are actually malicious scales.
And we see actually a number of real world incidents
of attacks on agents.
And it's rising fast.
And hence, what I want to emphasize here
is that as we increase in agent capability, autonomy,
and the set of privileges that agents have,
it's absolutely critical that we need to have stronger security
guarantees and to ensure a set of different types of security
goals including confidentiality integrity
availability, and also agent contextual security and privacy
to ensure that agents actions are aligned with user's intent.
In order to achieve this, we need
to develop new solutions for building secure agentic AI
systems.
And here, I will talk about technologies
for two stages, two main stages of the agentic AI system
development lifecycle.
The first one is on evaluation and risk assessment.
And the second one is on defenses.
So in order to build a secure agentic AI systems,
we first need to be able to do rigorous evaluation and risk
assessment so that we can actually
understand the different types of risks
and different potential attacks on any given AI systems.
So my group with collaborators, we
have had long journeys in this direction,
and we have been among the earliest
to develop, for example, the first comprehensive evaluation
framework for the trustworthiness
of large language models, for multi-models, for video models,
and also for overall agentic systems.
And many of these papers have won best paper awards and so on.
And here also is a overview of how we actually
think about the overall design space of automatic writing
for agentic AI.
For automatic writing for agentic AI,
essentially, we can think about the system as an optimization
loop for automatic attack generation, where
we can have these generators that uses different algorithms,
including machine learning models
and so on to automatically generate attack candidates.
And then these attack candidates are then
launched in the environments where the agent is interacting
and then getting feedback, and the feedback
can be used then further to update essentially the generator
for these attack candidates.
And this can be essentially automatic feedback loop
using different methods to optimize,
to generate more effective attack candidates.
So the different algorithms for these automatic optimization
loop can include, for example, search-based
and also, for example, evolution algorithm, genetic algorithms,
and also gradient-based, and also,
for example, reinforcement learning-based and so on.
And also this overall automated red teaming framework
can be agentic itself.
So essentially, we can build this automatic red teaming
agents to actually do automatic red teaming on a target AI
system.
And this is just a quick overview of the different types
of automatic writing agents, and also frameworks
that we have built using the different algorithms that I just
mentioned for agentic AI.
And also recently, together with other collaborators,
we have developed this unified platform
for agent writing called decoding trust
for agent platform, which has a large number
of simulated environments, allows agents to target agents
to run in the simulated environment,
and using this automated red teaming agents that I mentioned
to automatically then generate attack candidates
and continue to optimize it, and so on as well.
And with that, I also want to mention our most recent work
called the Super Red.
The goal of Super Red is actually
about developing an open ecosystem
for this type of automated red teaming
so that we can bring the community together
to build the best automated red teaming framework and system,
so that we can, overall, together
help improve the resilience of our agentic AI systems.
So the Super Red is designed as an open source framework that's
modularized, so you can bring in different attack algorithms.
You can bring in different evaluation benchmarks
and plug in different types of agent environments and so on.
So everything is modularized, and also fine grained
controlled modularized threat model as well.
And Super Red allows you to run any attacker against any AI
systems with any threat model.
And you can find out more information
on the Super Red website.
And currently, it comes in with 35 modules to run today.
And as the community contributes and plug
in new attack algorithms, new evaluation benchmarks,
and new environments, this will build the flywheel
to have the community together to build
this really powerful, open ecosystem for automated writing.
So we welcome everyone to check it out and contribute.
And with the system, you also get detailed runtime,
for example, observability, transparent insights,
and dashboards, and so on.
And it's really easy to install.
So really encourage the audience to go check it out.
So that's our evaluation.
Another important part, of course,
is actually building the AI defense itself.
And given the complexity of the issue,
there is no single silver bullet for building effective defense.
Instead, we need to deploy defense in depth
and also deploy and adopt best practice for security,
such as least privilege, privilege separation,
and by design to ensure that we in the end,
hopefully we can actually get a provably secure systems.
And again, in our paper, we actually
list out close to 20 different types of defense mechanisms
that you can use to build as a layered defense.
And also here is one example of our recent work called Progent,
which is the first programmable privileged control and guardrail
for agents with contextual security,
where we allow the guardrail to also automatically generate
dynamic security policies to dynamically reduce the agent's
privilege to achieve least privilege
with the contextual security.
So with that, that's the first part.
Building secure agentic AI to protect the agentic AI systems
from malicious attacks.
Now, let me quickly talk about the second part,
which is how we can actually mitigate misuse.
And in particular, in the space of cybersecurity.
So again, as I mentioned, there is a broad spectrum
of different types of AI risks.
But for me personally, I do strongly
believe that cybersecurity is one of the biggest AI risk
domains.
And this is also why my group would
have been among the earliest to actually working
to investigate the impact of frontier AI in landscape
cybersecurity.
And also with our work demonstrating the increased risk
in the space.
So the key question here is, how will frontier AI
change the landscape of cybersecurity, especially given
that AI is a dual use technology,
it can help both attacker side and defender side?
And in order to answer this question,
we need to actually do detailed analysis
through the complex kill chain for different stages of cyber
attacks and also for defenses.
And in order to achieve this, my group with our collaborators,
we have developed leading benchmarks
that has been used by essentially all frontier AI
labs on evaluating frontier capabilities in cybersecurity
that actually covers across the vulnerability lifecycle,
including vulnerability discovery, validation,
doing exploit generation, and also patching.
And with our CyberGym, which is a benchmark containing
large scale widely distributed open source software,
we showed that frontier AI's capability in cybersecurity
is increasing drastically.
And also within recent Claude Mythos and Project Glasswing
also further demonstrated the capabilities of frontier AI
capabilities in cyber.
And also with the recent exploitation,
also showing that the frontier AI now
can also automatically generate exploits,
and these exploits can even bypass existing
standard security mechanisms.
And also as many of you may have heard about the recent incidents
from OpenAI Hugging Face, the agent actually,
while trying to solve the exploitation
benchmark our benchmark actually
broke out of the isolation sandbox
from OpenAI's environment, and then actually, in the end,
did a very sophisticated attacks to actually in the end,
was able to break into Hugging Face infrastructure as well.
So all this illustrates that now, with the increased frontier
AI capabilities, the agents now have really strong capabilities
in cyber.
The agents, this was not even a misuse.
It was not a malicious attacker trying
to use agents to compromise another system.
The agents actually did this on its own.
So first of all, this told us that now,
with the agents' capabilities, even the evaluation
infrastructure itself are now becoming
part of the attack surface.
And also this really is a wake up call,
showing the power and the potential risk
these agent capability can bring to the world.
And in order to address all these issues,
so first we have launched a frontier AI separate security
observatory, bring the community together
to do continuous monitoring of the frontier
AI capabilities increase in cybersecurity.
And also a bigger question is, what can we do?
Especially given that AI, as a dual use technology,
it can help both attacker side and defender side.
And also the challenge here is that coding capabilities
and cyber capabilities are two sides of the same coin.
And what's even worse is that we call this equivalence class
problem.
Is that the same capabilities that can help defenders
essentially, in our paper, we show
that they can also be used by attackers
in the corresponding stage for attacks.
And furthermore, there is natural asymmetry
between defense and offense.
And for example, attackers only need
to find one successful vulnerability
and exploit and do a successful attack
to succeed where defenders need to defend against all attacks.
And also in our paper, we also show a number
of other natural asymmetries between attackers and defenders,
showing that unfortunately, due to this natural asymmetry,
in the near term, AI is going to help
attackers more than defenders.
So the question is, what can we do
to shift AI to help defenders more than attackers?
Throughout the history of cybersecurity community,
and also including my own work in the last two to three
decades, we have gone through three different paradigms
for building defenses.
The first one is reactive defense,
where defenders develop attack detection
and blocking mechanisms and also other mitigation mechanisms
after attacks has happened.
Unfortunately, with this defense paradigm, my belief is that,
and also our analysis shows that attackers can still benefit more
from AI than defenders.
And the second paradigm is proactive defense
through bug finding, where in this case,
the defenders can use AI to try to find bugs in code first
and then hope to fix them before attackers.
However, in this case, again, attacker also
can be at an advantage in the sense attackers only need
to find one successful attack.
So we really hope that with AI, it
can help us to achieve the first paradigm in a more effective
way, which is proactive defense through security
by construction.
Using this approach, we develop, we architect and build
provably secure programs and systems in contrast
to bug finding in attack detection
and reactive defense mechanisms.
And so through program verification
using formal verification, we hope that we can actually
build systems with provably secure guarantees that
can completely eliminate entire classes of vulnerabilities
and so on.
So this ultimately will put defenders in an advantage
to attackers.
And in fact, we have already entered
the era of formally verified systems
with many formally verified systems, including microkernels,
compilers, and so on.
But however, it's been labor intensive to actually do
the proof engineering for these systems,
and hence they have not been widely used.
And my group has been among the earliest, also
with our collaborators, to develop deep learning methods
for theorem proving.
And I strongly believe that now we are reaching an inflection
point.
Using frontier AI, we can further
enhance formal mathematical reasoning and automated theorem
proving.
We hope that using this approach,
instead of just generating code, we can actually
generate provably secure code, where
we combine the program synthesis with program verification.
And towards this goal, we also have
developed the current leading benchmarks for verifiable code
generation, including VERINA and Vero, which
now allows us to evaluate AI capabilities for verifying codes
at large scale repository level.
And we hope that with the community, together,
we can make rapid progress in this space.
And we can now finally use AI to help
shift the dynamics to help AI help
defenders more than attackers.
So with that, I want to conclude my talk.
And I want to just briefly want to mention
that besides this work, we also are developing
various work on open ecosystem for agent evaluation,
including Agents' Last Exam, a benchmark for evaluating agents
capabilities in real world economically
valuable long horizon tasks over 55 different sectors
and also agent beats for building a new standard
for open, standardized, reproducible agent evaluation.
And you can learn more on later today's workshop
on future of agent evaluation.
With that, thanks everyone.
